strengths: Clear diagnosis of basis misalignment as the root cause of gradient staleness sensitivity, with well-structured validation from toy problems to real models
Strong empirical results at tested scale: 71.6-81.6% iteration reduction and 1.27× slowdown vs. 4.24×+ for baselines; basis rotation restores scaling laws
Rigorous theoretical analysis with convergence bounds (Theorem 2.3) showing multiplicative interaction between delay τ and misalignment C
Practical framework with multiple approximation strategies and demonstrated wall-clock efficiency (54.3% GPU time savings)
Comprehensive experimental ablations including basis approximation quality, update frequency, weight stashing variations, and computational overhead analysis
weaknesses: Significant gap between problem scope and experimental validation: paper claims issue is critical for 100+ stages but only tests up to P=32; maximum model size 1B (modern LLMs are 7B-405B); no validation at production scale

Core assumptions not quantitatively validated: block-diagonal and Kronecker-factored Hessian structure claimed 'empirically supported' but no empirical characterization of how well these hold in transformers or degradation when violated

Restrictive theoretical assumptions (coordinate-wise ℓ∞ smoothness, β₁=0) with loose convergence bounds that don't provide actionable guidance on when basis rotation is necessary; the (1,1)-norm proxy for misalignment lacks empirical validation of correlation with actual convergence

Limited experimental scope: single task (language modeling), single architecture (transformers), relatively short training runs, no benchmark evaluation (e.g., perplexity), no comparison of interaction with other parallelism strategies (tensor/data parallelism)
Computational overhead under-characterized: power iteration cost, memory cost of eigenvector storage, and scaling behavior to large models not analyzed; basis update frequency sensitivity limited

Incremental methodological novelty: basis rotation builds heavily on recent optimizers (SOAP, GaLore); main contribution is diagnosis and application to async pipeline parallelism rather than new techniques

Theoretical-practice gap: spiral loss landscape (Section 2.2) is synthetic; no empirical proof that (1,1)-norm predicts slowdown in real transformers; convergence bound doesn't guide when the (1+τ) delay factor becomes prohibitive

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear empirical evidence that delay scales with pipeline depth (5.81× slowdown), addressing a real bottleneck in large-scale LLM training

Novel insight connecting basis misalignment to Adam's vulnerability to gradient delay, formalized through convergence analysis (Theorem 2.3) showing multiplicative interaction between delay τ and basis misalignment C
Comprehensive multi-layered empirical validation from synthetic examples (quadratic, spiral landscape) to real LLM pre-training with convincing results (81.7% iteration reduction on 3B model)

Principled solution design with multiple eigenbasis-estimation strategies offering flexibility and efficiency through Kronecker factorization and practical stage-aware allocation (29.2% additional speedup)

Thorough experimental analysis including ablations on basis approximation strategies (Figure 8), robustness without weight stashing (Figure 10), wall-clock efficiency (Figure 9a), and generalization to MoE architectures
Clear presentation with effective use of figures (especially Figures 3-4) to illustrate basis alignment effects, comprehensive appendices with full proofs
weaknesses: Limited novelty: Core basis rotation technique exists in SOAP, GaLore, and others; primary contribution is application to asynchronous pipeline parallelism, which is somewhat incremental

Restrictive theoretical assumptions: coordinate-wise ℓ∞ smoothness (Assumption 2.2) is stronger than standard smoothness; main Theorem 2.3 uses β₁=0 despite practical β₁=0.9; dimension-dependent terms make convergence bound O(√(1+dτ)R/T) very loose for high-dimensional problems (d~10,000)

Limited experimental scale: maximum 3B parameters (1B training only in main experiments) is modest for ICML 2026; virtual GPU staging doesn't replicate real distributed training across multiple nodes with actual communication patterns

Hessian approximation assumptions may not hold exactly in practice: Kronecker factorization assumed for Transformers, S=1st strategy assumes H=E[g]E[g]⊤ (acknowledged as not faithful), single-step power iteration approximation quality not quantified

Reproducibility concerns: code link incomplete on page 1; missing implementation details including initialization of rotation matrices, eigenvalue degeneracy handling, and interaction with layer normalization

Marginal improvement over related work: comparison with SOAP (Table 3) shows 1.27× vs 1.34× slowdown—only marginal difference despite dramatic 81.7% improvement claim against weaker baselines like PipeDream

Practical deployment gaps: no evaluation with orthogonal parallelism strategies (data, tensor parallelism used in practice); memory overhead can be substantial (1.66GB per layer for bilateral strategy); no analysis of interaction with gradient compression/quantization
